questions.text: Beata has two dolls, three apples, one chocolate bar, two oranges, five peaches, and one bike. How many pieces of fruit does Beata have?
questions.solution:
List only the fruit items:
- apples: 3
- oranges: 2
- peaches: 5
Dolls, the chocolate bar, and the bike are NOT fruit, so ignore them.
Total fruit = 3 + 2 + 5 = 10.
methods: Add only the fruit counts and skip non-fruit objects
questions.diagram: A simple grouping picture separating fruit (apples, oranges, peaches) from non-fruit (dolls, chocolate, bike).
questions.tip: Read carefully: only count fruit, not every object mentioned.

questions.text: What number is in the part that is common to four circles? (A central region where all four overlapping circles overlap contains a number.)
questions.solution:
The region common to all four circles is the single central overlap where every circle meets.
Look at the number placed in that central shared region of the diagram.
That number is 6, so the value in the part common to all four circles is 6.
methods: Identify the central intersection of all four circles and read its label
questions.diagram: Four overlapping circles; the central region shared by all four shows the number 6.
questions.tip: The 'common to four circles' region is only the very center where all four overlap, not the other overlaps.

questions.text: In how many places do we need to break a wooden stick in order to get 5 pieces?

options.E: It depends on how long the stick is.

questions.solution:
Each break increases the number of pieces by 1.
Start with 1 piece (the whole stick).
After 1 break -> 2 pieces.
After 2 breaks -> 3 pieces.
After 3 breaks -> 4 pieces.
After 4 breaks -> 5 pieces.
So we need 4 breaks to make 5 pieces. This does not depend on the stick's length.
methods: Count that each break adds exactly one piece, so pieces = breaks + 1
questions.diagram: A stick drawn with 4 cut marks producing 5 equal segments.
questions.tip: Common mistake: thinking 5 pieces need 5 breaks. Remember pieces = breaks + 1.

questions.text: Karl is now 10 years old, and Alice is 3 years old. How many years from now will Karl be twice as old as Alice?
questions.solution:
Let x = number of years from now.
Karl's age then: 10 + x
Alice's age then: 3 + x
We want Karl to be twice Alice's age:
10 + x = 2(3 + x)
10 + x = 6 + 2x
Subtract x from both sides: 10 = 6 + x
Subtract 6: x = 4
Check: in 4 years Karl is 14, Alice is 7, and 14 = 2 x 7. Correct.
methods: Set up equation 10+x = 2(3+x) and solve
Test the answer choices by checking each
questions.diagram: A small table: years from now | Karl | Alice | twice Alice?
questions.tip: Set up an equation with x years; both ages grow by the same amount.

questions.text: Anna and her sister Barbara go to the same school, but take two different ways (two grid paths between the same two points). Whose way is shorter?

options.D: Both ways have the same length.

questions.solution:
On a square grid, moving along the grid lines, the length of a path is the number of unit steps.
Both paths go between the same start and end points using only horizontal and vertical grid moves.
Count the steps: each path must move the same number of units right/left and up/down to connect the same two points, so both paths have the same total length.
methods: Count unit grid steps on each path and compare
questions.diagram: Two different grid routes between the same two corners, each made of the same number of unit segments.
questions.tip: On a grid, any monotone path between two points has the same length if it only uses right/up (or equivalent) moves.

questions.text: Our class has 30 students. The number of boys is four times the number of girls. How many girls are there?
questions.solution:
Let g = number of girls.
Then boys = 4g.
Total students: g + 4g = 30
5g = 30
g = 6
So there are 6 girls (and 24 boys).
Check: 6 + 24 = 30, and 24 is four times 6.
methods: Use g + 4g = 30
Think of 5 equal parts of 30, one part is girls
questions.diagram: A bar split into 5 equal parts: 1 part girls, 4 parts boys, total 30.
questions.tip: Set the smaller group as 1 part; the total is 5 parts.

questions.text: How much does the orange weigh? (Balance puzzle: an apple plus an orange balances 255 g; an apple plus two oranges balances 410 g.)
questions.solution:
Let A = weight of apple, O = weight of orange.
From the first balance: A + O = 255
From the second balance: A + 2O = 410
Subtract the first equation from the second:
(A + 2O) - (A + O) = 410 - 255
O = 155
So the orange weighs 155 g.
methods: Subtract the two balance equations to remove the apple
Compare both pans: adding one orange adds 155 g
questions.diagram: Two balance scales: left pan apple+orange = 255g; left pan apple+2 oranges = 410g.
questions.tip: Compare the two balances: the extra orange accounts for the extra weight.

questions.text: The cat says, 'The length of my tail is 12 cm and half the length of my tail.' How long is the cat's tail?
questions.solution:
Let L = length of the tail.
The cat says: L = 12 + (1/2)L
Subtract (1/2)L from both sides: (1/2)L = 12
Multiply by 2: L = 24
So the tail is 24 cm long.
Check: half of 24 is 12, and 12 + 12 = 24.
methods: Solve L = 12 + L/2
Notice '12 and half the tail' means 12 equals the other half
questions.diagram: A tail split into two halves: one half labeled 12 cm, the other half also 12 cm.
questions.tip: If 12 cm is half the tail, the whole tail is double that.

questions.text: Mom's birthday is on a Sunday. Dad's birthday is 55 days later. On what day of the week is dad's birthday?
questions.solution:
A week has 7 days, so we work modulo 7.
55 days = 7 x 7 + 6 = 49 + 6, so 55 mod 7 = 6.
55 days later is the same as 6 days later in the week.
Sunday + 6 days: Mon(1), Tue(2), Wed(3), Thu(4), Fri(5), Sat(6).
So dad's birthday is on a Saturday.
methods: Compute 55 mod 7 = 6, then add 6 days to Sunday
Count weeks: 7 weeks (49 days) brings back to Sunday, plus 6 more days
questions.diagram: A 7-day week strip showing Sunday then counting 6 steps forward to Saturday.
questions.tip: Only the remainder when divided by 7 matters for the day of the week.

questions.text: Two basketball teams play a tournament. The first team to win 4 games wins the tournament. There are no ties. What is the greatest possible number of games?
questions.solution:
The tournament ends as soon as one team reaches 4 wins.
To make the tournament as long as possible, the two teams should be as close as possible.
The longest case: one team gets its 4th win on the final game, while the other team has 3 wins.
Total games = 4 + 3 = 7.
(Example: wins go A,B,A,B,A,B,A -> A wins 4-3 in 7 games.)
It cannot be 8 because after 7 games someone must have at least 4 wins.
methods: Max games = 4 + (4-1) = 7
If 8 games were played, one team would have at least 4 wins earlier
questions.diagram: A scoreboard showing wins 4 to 3 after 7 games.
questions.tip: The loser can win at most one fewer than the winner; add the two totals.

questions.text: Instead of adding 27 to a number, John subtracted 27. What is the difference between his result and the correct result?
questions.solution:
Let the number be n.
Correct result: n + 27
John's result: n - 27
Difference: (n + 27) - (n - 27) = n + 27 - n + 27 = 54
So the difference is 54.
(It is the same for any n.)
methods: Subtract the two expressions: (n+27)-(n-27)=54
Try n=0: correct 27, John's -27, difference 54
questions.diagram: A number line showing n, then n+27 and n-27, with the gap of 54 between them.
questions.tip: Adding instead of subtracting (or vice versa) by k changes the answer by 2k.

questions.text: A golden cube with edge 4 cm is cut into small cubes with edge 1 cm. How many small cubes are there?
questions.solution:
Along each edge of the big cube we can fit 4 / 1 = 4 small cubes.
So the big cube is 4 small cubes long, 4 wide, and 4 high.
Total small cubes = 4 x 4 x 4 = 64.
(Equivalently, volume of big cube = 4x4x4 = 64 cm^3; each small cube = 1 cm^3; 64 / 1 = 64.)
methods: 4 x 4 x 4 layered counting
Compare volumes: 64 cm^3 / 1 cm^3 = 64
questions.diagram: A 4x4x4 grid of small cubes forming the large cube.
questions.tip: In three dimensions, multiply the number along each edge; don't just do 4 x 4.
